paragraphs: Aboda zara ben shel yisrael uben shel nakeri asura bahanaa vaapillu im nisrepa asur lehanot begachaltah veeprah veken tashmishe aboda zara venoy shellah vetiqrabettah kullam asurim ezehu goy veezehu tiqrobet? hinneh kol nerot shemmadliqin lepaneha veken begadim vekelim naim sheshshochatim lepaneha o malbishim otah vetolin lah hare zeh noy vehattiqrobet hu kol dabar shekkayyotze bo qareb al gabbe hammizbeach kegon basar ushemanim uselatot umayim umelach shehinnichu lepaneha leshem tiqrobet neesar miyyad abal dabar sheen maqribin mimmenna al gabbe hammizbeach kegon besar chayya veop eno neesar bammeh debarim amurim bemannicha lepaneha abal im shachat lepaneha apillu chayya veop sheen qerebin al gabbe hammizbeach neesar biklal tiqrobet vaapillu im shachat chagab lepaneha neesar v"p sheen abodatam bekak:

clarification.explanation: An idol (whether made by a Jew or a gentile) is entirely forbidden for benefit, and even its ash and embers after burning are forbidden, as are its accessories, ornaments, and offerings. An "ornament" is, for example, candles lit before it or garments dressed on it. An "offering" (forbidden immediately) is something of the type offered on the altar (meat, oil, fine flour, water, salt) placed before it for worship; something not of the altar-offering type (a wild animal, a fowl) does not become forbidden merely by being placed before it, but if slaughtered before it — it becomes forbidden (even a locust).
takeaways: An idol, its ornaments, and its accessories are entirely forbidden for benefit, including its ash and embers.
An item "offered" to an idol (mainly by slaughter) becomes forbidden even if it is not of the type normally sacrificed.

paragraphs: Bazzeman hazzeh kol hatztzurot hannimtzaim ben bikparim ben bakkerakkim im nikkar haddabar shennaasu leshem aboda zara asurim veken tzurat sheti vaereb shemmaamidin bebet kenesiyya shellahem bipnim dino kaaboda zara mammash shehare mekabbedin otam veken kol sheti vaereb shemmannichin bekol maqom, im mekabbedin otam, shelloqechin hakkoba umishtachavin lahem dinam kaaboda zara mammash abal tzurat sheti vaereb shettolin al hatztzavvar vekayyotze ellu naasin lezikkaron velo niqreu tzelem veen lahem din aboda zara veayyen chakemat adam kelal p"z seip ' yeuyyan sham:

clarification.explanation: In our time, figures recognizably made for idolatrous purposes are forbidden. A cross (crosswise) placed in a church that people honor has the law of an actual idol. A cross worn on the neck merely as a keepsake (with no honor/bowing) is not considered an "image" and has no idol status.
takeaways: A cross honored in worship (in a church, with bowing) is an actual idol; a cross worn as mere personal jewelry for remembrance is not forbidden.

paragraphs: Bazzeman haqqodem hayu aduqim baaboda zara vehayu choqeqim tzurat aboda zara al kele tashmisham vehayu obedim leotam hatztzurot velaken kelim hamkubbadim shel zeman haqqodem kegon mine takshitin ubigde meshi veriqma shennimtza alehem tzurot, setaman hare ellu naasu leshem aboda zara vaasurin bahanaa veraq im yadua lanu shello naasu leshem aboda zara muttarim abal kelim hambuzzim kegon shettashmishan baakila ushetiyya im nimtzeu alehem tzurot setaman shello naasu leshem aboda zara velo hayu obedin d"p deotah tzura neebedet kevan shehi al kelim mebuzzim vadday lo hayu obedin otam veken tzurot hannimtzaim al hammatbeot chezqatam shello naasu leshem aboda zara umuttarim vekol kelim shehem sapeq im nechshabim mebuzzin o mekubbadim im nimtza alehem tzura shenneebda hare ellu asurim missapeq veyesh machmirin yoter usebira lehu kol sheyyadua sheotah hatztzura neebedet "p shehi nimtzet al kelim hambuzzim asur, veraq im yesh sapeq betzura dela yadeinan im obedin leotah tzura o lav az haddin hu im nimtzet al hamkubbadin asura missapeq veim nimtzet al hambuzzin mutteret:

Vekol zeh al hannimtza miyyamim qadmonim shehayu aduqim baaboda zara abal bazzeman hazzeh en aduqim baaboda zara velaken tzurat sheti vaereb sheyyesh lahem bazzeman hazzeh "p dekatabnu leel deotam tzurot sheti vaereb shemmannichim otam bipnim dimkabbedin otam umishtachavim lahem dedinam kaaboda zara mammash mikkol maqom tzurat sheti vaereb sheosim al hakkelim veken tzurat ishsha meniqa ubenah "p sheosim otam al kelim mekubbadim kegon takshitin vekayyotze en osin otam ella lenoy velizkaro veen mishtachavim lahem velaken muttarim bahanaa abal asur leyisrael lehashhotan etzlo im hem boletin veayyen chakemat adam kelal p" seip b' yeuyyan sham:

clarification.explanation: In ancient times, when people were devoted to idolatry, honored vessels (jewelry, silk garments) bearing figures were presumed to have been made for idolatry and forbidden for benefit, unless known otherwise; but debased vessels (used for eating/drinking) bearing figures were presumed not to have been worshiped, since surely people would not worship something debased; and figures on coins were presumed not made for idolatry, and are permitted. Vessels in doubt whether honored or debased, on which a figure known to have been worshiped was found, are forbidden out of doubt. Some are stricter, holding that anything known with certainty to be a worshiped figure is forbidden even on debased vessels (not relying on the reasoning that people would surely not worship something debased); and only when there is doubt whether the figure itself was ever worshiped does the law depend on the vessel type — forbidden out of doubt on honored vessels, permitted on debased ones. In our time (when people are not devoted to idolatry), crosswise figures on vessels (and even a figure of a nursing woman and her child) on jewelry — for mere ornament, are permitted for benefit, but it is forbidden to keep them if they are raised/protruding.
takeaways: In ancient times: honored vessels with figures were suspected of idolatry; debased vessels and coins were presumed permitted.

A stricter view: a figure known with certainty to have been worshiped is forbidden even on debased vessels; the debased-vessel leniency applies only when it is doubtful the figure itself was ever worshiped.
In our time: religious figures on jewelry are for ornament, permitted for benefit, but raised/protruding figures may not be kept.

paragraphs: "p shekkatabnu tzurat sheti vaereb shettolin al hatztzavvar naasu lezikkaron bealema veen lahem din aboda zara umuttarim mikkol maqom tzurat sheti vaereb shettolin hakkemarim al bigdehem o al tzavvaram yesh lehachmir veayyen chakemat adam seip ':

clarification.explanation: Although a cross worn on the neck merely as a keepsake is permitted, a cross worn by priests on their garments or neck should be treated stringently (there, actual honor is a genuine concern).
takeaways: A cross on priests' garments (unlike personal jewelry) should be treated stringently.

paragraphs: Mitzva al kol yisrael hammotze aboda zara sheyyebaarenna viabbedenna velipamim yimtza chatikot shel nechoshet o kesep vezahab o eben vekayyotze veyesh alehem tzurot yeshanot veqorin otam annetikah (antiqa, utqeh), im nikkar bah siman shennaaset lezikkaron mikkoach hakketiba shennimtzet aleha let lan bah, abal im nikkar bah ezeh siman shello naaset lezikkaron ella hi aboda zara chayyab kol yisrael habbaa leyado lebaarah uleabbedah min haolam ubeare innadya (hodu) gam bazzeman hazzeh yimmatze sham obede aboda zara sheobedim leetz veeben vechayyab kol yisrael shettabo leyado aboda zara shellahem lebaarah uleabbedah:

clarification.explanation: Every Jew who finds an idol is commanded to destroy and eliminate it. Ancient pieces (copper, silver, gold, stone) with old figures ("antiques"): if it is recognizable they were made for mere remembrance (from an inscription on them), they are permitted; if it is recognizable they are an actual idol, they must be destroyed. In India, where idol-worshipers still exist, one must destroy an idol that comes into a Jew's possession.
takeaways: Antiques with figures: if clearly for remembrance, permitted; if actual idols, must be destroyed.

paragraphs: Ketzad mebaarah shocheq vezoreh larucha o layyam o zoreq otah layyam apillu belo shechiqa dezeh hu ibbudah deen chashash sheyyimtzaenna acher vehu haddin limshammesheha venoyah shetztzarik leabbedam beopen zeh, shenneemar abad teabbedun vehalloqechah lebeto ober mishshum lo tabi toeba el beteka, apillu maknisah lepi shaa:

clarification.explanation: The manner of destroying an idol: grinding it and scattering it to the wind or the sea, or throwing it into the sea even without grinding — so it is never found again. The same applies to its accessories and ornaments. It is forbidden to bring an idol into one's house even for a brief moment ("you shall not bring an abomination into your house").
takeaways: Destroying an idol means grinding and scattering to wind/sea; it is forbidden to bring it into one's house even for a moment.

paragraphs: Im baim liqnot miyyisrael dabar letzorek hashsheti veereb o bishbil noy shello asur limkor lahem veken hu haddin im qonin mimmennu dabar laasoto likbod hashsheti veereb shemmunnach bebet kenisatam bipnim, hen zekukit vetzeba hen nerot vekayyotze - asur limkor lahem veap al gab deyesh omerim im epshar lahem liqnot zeh meacher muttar limkor lahem - rauy lehachmir bekol gavna vehannizhar bazeh yishshaer beraka meet Adonai baolam shekkullo tob:

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to sell gentiles anything for the sake of their cross or to adorn their house of worship (glass, paint, candles), even though some permit it if they could buy it elsewhere — it is proper to always be stringent.
takeaways: One should not sell gentiles items for their worship, even if they could obtain them elsewhere.

paragraphs: Asur leyisrael lilbosh begadim sheyyesh bahem sheti vaereb baariga shehem boletim abal im en bolet muttar veken asur laasot betziyyur vekiyyor shebbebeto tzurat sheti vaereb hen beetzim shel delatot veshel kotalim vetiqra hen bebinyan haabanim im hu bolet, vehaynu davqa dearbaa rashim shel hashsheti veereb hem mebuddalim bipne atzmam babbelita shellahem, veenam mechubbarim veniknasim bedabar acher, abal im rashe hashsheti veereb niknasim bachalaqim acherim veshavim immahem sheenam boletim veyotzeim alehem muttar veen bazeh chashash:

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden for a Jew to wear a garment with a raised (protruding) cross pattern (but not raised — permitted). Likewise, one should not design a raised cross shape in a house (in door woodwork, in the building), specifically when the cross's four ends are separate and protrude on their own; if integrated with other parts and not protruding, it is permitted.
takeaways: A raised cross shape (on a garment or in a building) is forbidden; non-protruding/integrated shapes are permitted.

paragraphs: Ketib lo taasun itti elohe kesep veku', veqibbelu chaza"l dehizhir hakkatub shello letzayyer tzurat arbaa panim shebbammerkaba bahade hadade dehaynu pene shor veadam vearyeh venesher lechayya achat dugmat chayyot haqqodesh "p sheoseh otam lenoy bealema veken tzurat adam asur letzayyer apillu lebaddo veen immo shear tzurot shebbammerkaba vaapillu oseh oto lenoy bealema vaapillu eno oseh leatzmo ella bishbil nakeri name asur ukeshem sheasur laasotan kak asur lomar lenakeri laasotam daamira lenakeri shebut. veim hannakeri asa otah meelayv leyisrael asur leyisrael lehashhotam etzlo:

Bammeh debarim amurim betzura boletet abal beshoqaat muttar umikkol maqom nakon lehachmir gam beshoqaat, lachush lisbarat haramba"n vehara"n za"l deaseri beshoqaat, ak pashat hamminhag lehattir beshoqaat veen limchot bazeh vetzura hannaaset betzeba ab, nireh bah belita veasur abal tzeba qal kemo deyo al hanneyar let lan bah. veda ki bazzeman hazzeh loqechim tzurat haadam kemo shehi "y hamakkina (mekona) hachadasha hannaaset byrvp" sheqqure pvtvgr"p (tatzlum) vezo adipa mitztzeba qal al neyar sheen bah belita apillu mashshehu venitpashsheta melaka zo bekol haolam vedashu bah rabbim v"g degam bazeh yesh middat chasidut mikkol maqom im yesh tzorek gadol baddabar yiqqechu tzurat hahipnim bilbad belo yadayim veraglayim veaz gam adam chashub en lo lachush bekak umaaseh shellaqechu tzurat chakamim bimlaka zo tzurat happanim bilbad veamarti leechad en lo leharher bazeh kevan dela matza yadayv veraglayv bebet hammidrash, vekol shekken heka dehaya tzorek gadol bekak:

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to draw the four faces of the divine chariot together (ox, man, lion, eagle) even merely as ornament; a human figure alone (without the other figures) is also forbidden to draw, even as ornament, even for a gentile, and even telling a gentile to make it is forbidden. And even if the gentile made the human figure on his own initiative, without the Jew asking, it is forbidden for the Jew to keep it in his possession. A raised figure is forbidden; a sunken (engraved inward) figure is permitted by law, though it is proper to be stringent about it too — and the widespread custom is to permit it, with no protest. Thick paint (creating a raised effect) is forbidden; light paint/ink is permitted. Modern photography is preferable to painting, since it has no raised effect at all; and in great need, even a face-only photograph (without hands and feet) is permitted even for an important person.
takeaways: Drawing the four chariot faces together, or a complete raised human figure, is forbidden even as ornament and even for a gentile.
Even if a gentile made a human figure on his own initiative, a Jew may not keep it.
A face-only photograph (without limbs) is permitted even for an important person in need.

paragraphs: Tzurat haadam deasur beboletet haynu apillu shehu eno shalem ella mitztzad happanim veen bo tzad haachor daapillu deen asuy kol haggup shalem panim veachor name asur abal im tzad happanim atzmo eno shalem sheen bo ella raq tzurat harosh bilbad veen bo yadayim veraglayim muttar apillu bebolet veken im hu chatzi gup keadam hashshokeb al tziddo sheen bo ella ayin achat veozen achat vachatzi chotem veyad achat veregel achat muttar appayv bolet veyesh choleqin veoserin bekol gavna bebolet vekevan shehu issur tora yesh lehachmir kisbarat haoserin:

clarification.explanation: The prohibition of a raised human figure applies even if it is only the front (without the back). But if the front itself is incomplete (only a head without hands and feet), it is permitted even raised. Likewise a half-body (like a person lying on their side, one eye, one ear) is permitted even raised (some disagree and forbid, and it is proper to be stringent).
takeaways: A partial human figure (head only, or half-body) is by law permitted even raised, but in practice one should be stringent and forbid it, since this is a Torah-level prohibition.

paragraphs: Akku"m haoseh mishteh lenissue beno o bitto umazmin layyehudim leekol immo "p shehayyehudim okelim mishshellahem vehammeshammeshin gam ken mishshellahem im kol zeh asur diktib veqara leka veakalta mizzibcho lamad im qaraaka vehizmineka laakila "p sheakalta mishshelleka nechshab leka akilat mizzibcho vaapillu meyached cheder meyuchad layyehudim lebaddam asur mihu zeh eno ella im mazmino lisuda shel mishteh vesimcha sheorek shulchan im perot veshekar abal im en haggoy mebi ella raq kos shel qhvv"y (qapeh) vachatikat matoq kederek shemmebiin lehabbaim laasot vzyt" (biqqur nimusin) let lan bah vegam od eno asur ella hazmana shel mishteh nissuin beno o bitto abal belav haki muttar mihu kol sheoseh hasseuda tok sheloshim yom qodem nissuin veken tok sheloshim yom achar nesuim asur veillu hizmino bistam asur abal achar sheloshim yom, im amar lo beperush shemmazmino bishbil hannissuin asur veim bistam shari:

clarification.explanation: A gentile who holds a feast for his son's/daughter's wedding and invites Jews — it is forbidden to participate (even eating one's own food), since the invitation itself is considered "eating from his sacrifice" — even in a separate room. This applies specifically to a feast with fruits and beer; a courtesy visit with only coffee and sweets is permitted. This prohibition applies within thirty days before/after the wedding (for a plain invitation); after thirty days — only if he explicitly said the invitation is for the wedding.
takeaways: A gentile's wedding feast (30 days before/after) forbids Jewish participation; a light courtesy visit (coffee) is permitted.

paragraphs: En moserin tinoq yisrael laggoy lelammedo seper ulelammedo ummanut apillu bemaqom deen lachush lishpikut damim ki yesh lachush shemma yimmashek achar minut veod yesh lachush lemishkab zekur v"p sheameru al tinoq demashma sheodennu qatan shello higgia legadlut shel y"g shana veyom echad im kol tzarik lehizzaher kol heka daadayin en lo chatimat zaqan:

clarification.explanation: One should not hand over a Jewish child to a gentile for book learning or a trade (even with no concern of mortal danger), out of concern he might be drawn toward heresy or homosexual relations — until he is a bearded adult (mature).
takeaways: A Jewish child should not be handed to a gentile for study, out of concern for negative influence, until adulthood.

paragraphs: En holekin bechuqqot haggoyim velo medammin lahem vekol beged hamyuchad laggoyim upereshu hayyehudim mimmennu mechamat tzeniut o dabar acher hare zeh asur layyehudim lilbosh kamohu ki kevan shennityached lahem mippene goyutan upereshu hayyehudim mimmennu mippene yahadutan az keshellobeshim oto hayyehudim nireh kemodeh lahem venimshak acharehem, veken tzarik shello yaaseh kammaasim hamyuchadim lahem kegon minhagam shennohagim leqanneach et haeber bakkotel achar hahashtana veken minhagam beseder harechitza sherochatzim bammayim qodem tepillatam lehannicha mayim bimqomot hayyeduim lahem sheyyesh lahem choq bidbarim ellu vekol kayyotze bazeh:

clarification.explanation: One should not follow the customs of gentiles or resemble them. A garment specific to gentiles, from which Jews have distanced themselves (out of modesty or another reason) — it is forbidden for Jews to wear it (it appears as agreement with them). One should not adopt customs unique to gentiles (such as special cleaning/washing arrangements specific to them).
takeaways: One should not resemble gentiles in distinctive dress and customs that Jews have specifically distanced themselves from.

paragraphs: Lo yigdal tzitzit rosho ketzitzit rosham velo yegalleh rosho kemo gillucha shellahem velaken lo yegalleach emtza harosh ulehannicha min hatztzedadin missabib belo gillucha o yegalleach min hatztzedadin veyannicha haemtza belo gillucha ki kol zeh hayeta chuqqot haakku"m mizzeman qadmon veayyen beseper arama beperush haramba"m za"l:

clarification.explanation: One should not grow head hair like them nor shave the head in their manner (for example, shaving the middle and leaving the sides, or vice versa) — these were ancient idol-worshipers' customs.
takeaways: Certain haircut styles (shaving the middle/sides) are forbidden as ancient gentile customs.

paragraphs: Mechuqqot haggoyim lehitztaer al metehem ad shettoleshin searam vesoretin bibsaram veim yisrael oseh ken hare zeh loqeh mishshum veseret lenepesh vetzarik lehazhir hannashim bazeh shello yitleshu searah mittok tzaaram al hammet ubashsheni searot chayyab mishshum qarecha ubesear echad ikka issur tora sheggam hannashim muzharot al zeh veken muzharot besarat shessoretin bibsaram mechamat tzaaram al hammet v"g shechiyyub malqot lekka ella besoret al met mikkol maqom issura ikka apillu besoret al shear mine tzaar vekannizkar beshulchan aruk siman q"p veod mechuqqotehem hu shessoretim bibsaram umemalleim hasseret bemin tzeba o bidyo o shetztzobea techilla vech"k soret, veyisrael haoseh ken chayyab malqut diktib uketubbat qaaqa veku' umikkol maqom muttar litten eper maqleh al hammakka lirpua "p shennishar haroshem demakkato mokachat alayv sheeno oseh mishshum chuqqot haggoyim vekannizkar beshulchan aruk:

clarification.explanation: It is a gentile custom to grieve over the dead to the point of tearing out hair and scratching the flesh; a Jew who does so transgresses "and you shall not gash yourselves." Women especially should be warned. Tearing out two hairs from grief is liable for baldness; one hair — a Torah prohibition (for women too). Scratching from grief (even not over a dead person) is forbidden, though lashes apply only regarding a dead person. A tattoo (scratching with dye) carries a lash liability; but it is permitted to place ash on a wound for medicine, even though a mark remains (since it is recognizable as medicine, not a custom).
takeaways: Tearing hair or scratching flesh from grief over the dead is forbidden (especially severe), as is tattooing.
Ash placed on a wound for medicine, even leaving a mark, is permitted (recognizably medicinal, not a custom).

paragraphs: En menachashin benichushin degoyim shenneemar lo tenachashu kegon ellu sheomerim hoil venapela pitto mippiv o maqlo miyyado enennu holek lemaqom peloni hayyom, shello yatzlicha veken kayyotze middibre shetut kaelleh, veken haomerim shachatu tarnegolet zo sheqqara ketarnegol veyesh omerim davqa lomar ken beperush asur abal lishchot bistam muttar veyesh omerim daapillu lomar beperush muttar degoresin baggemara bazeh en bo darke haemori vehammeqel lishchot bistam yesh lo al mah lismok vehabboteach baAdonai chesed yesobebennu:

clarification.explanation: One should not practice divination like the gentiles, as it says "you shall not divine" — such as those who say "since my bread fell from my mouth, or my staff from my hand, I will not go today to such-and-such place since I will not succeed" and similar foolish statements; and likewise those who say "slaughter this hen that crowed like a rooster." There is a dispute here: some say specifically stating this explicitly is forbidden, but slaughtering plainly (without stating it) is permitted; and some say even stating it explicitly is permitted (reading in the Gemara "there is no Amorite custom in it"). One who is lenient to slaughter plainly has grounds to rely upon — "and one who trusts in the Lord, kindness surrounds him."
takeaways: It is forbidden to practice gentile-style divination ("my bread fell — I won't go"), and likewise regarding a hen that crowed like a rooster.
There is a dispute whether explicit statement alone is forbidden or even that is permitted; one who is lenient to slaughter plainly has grounds to rely upon.
